short_title: Re: Resolution Dated August 30, 2017 in OMB-C-C-13-0357 v. Atty. Talaboc
full_title: RE: RESOLUTION DATED AUGUST 30, 2017 IN OMB-C-C-13-0357, ETC., COMPLAINANT, VS. ATTY. EDITHA P. TALABOC, ATTY. DELFIN R. AGCAOILI, JR., AND ATTY. MARK S. OLIVEROS, RESPONDENTS.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > A. Legal Ethics (CPRA) > 9. Discipline and Disbarment of Lawyers (Canon VI) > e. Burden of Proof and Quantum of Evidence
topics: Substantial evidence and the lawyer's presumption of innocence in disciplinary cases
Notary not liable where signatures and seals were forged (Rigon v. Subia distinguished)
Failure to answer is not an admission
Disregard of IBP-CBD directives as a less serious offense under the CPRA
Mitigating and aggravating circumstances (CPRA Canon VI, Secs. 38-39)
doctrine:
**In disciplinary proceedings, the lawyer is presumed innocent and presumed to have performed his or her duties in accordance with the oath; the complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence** (Rule 133, Sec. 6 of the Rules on Evidence). Mere allegations, conjectures and suppositions are not proof, and the respondent's failure to answer the complaint is not an admission of its allegations (reiterated).

A notary public is **not liable** for notarizations made in his or her name where there is substantial evidence that the signatures were forged and the notarial certificates themselves are irregular (missing the commission serial number, office address, IBP chapter or place of issue of the PTR; commission periods and IBP/PTR receipts that do not match official records), casting doubt on the validity of the seals and stamps used. Negligence in safekeeping the notarial paraphernalia cannot then be inferred: "Notaries are not immune from identity theft." The Court distinguished *Rigon v. Atty. Subia* (notary accountable for his seal where he did not deny its authenticity) and cases where negligence was shown by giving secretaries full access to the notarial paraphernalia or by entries in the notarial books. Given the proliferation of fake notaries, liability for alleged violations of the Notarial Rules is determined **case by case**.

Separately, **failing to comply with the IBP-CBD's directives** (to answer, attend the mandatory conference and file a position paper) **violates Canon III, Sec. 2 of the CPRA** and is a **less serious offense under Canon VI, Sec. 34(c)**, sanctioned under Sec. 37(b). A first offense is mitigating (Sec. 38(a)(1)), allowing a fine of not less than half the minimum (PHP 17,500.00) under Sec. 39; previous administrative liability is aggravating, allowing a penalty up to double the maximum.
facts:
Criminal complaints for plunder, graft, malversation through falsification and other offenses were filed with the Office of the Ombudsman (OMB) in OMB-C-C-13-0357 over the release and liquidation of PHP 900 million of the Malampaya Fund. The complainants there alleged that the memoranda of agreement used were "notarized" by Ben Hur Luy, who forged the signatures of respondents Attys. Editha P. Talaboc, Delfin R. Agcaoili, Jr. and Mark S. Oliveros and used their registers, stamps and seals; that Atty. Oliveros, Janet Lim Napoles's wedding godson, knew of the use of his name and was paid; and that the notarial details of the two others were supplied by one Tess Rodino. The OMB found that respondents did not notarize the documents and that there was insufficient proof they knew of or were part of the scheme, but recommended disciplinary action for allowing the use of their signatures, seals and registers for a fee. The matter was forwarded to the Court and referred to the IBP.

Only Atty. Agcaoili answered. He denied notarizing the documents, said he kept his notarial paraphernalia in a locked drawer, and pointed out that in the NBI investigation Luy admitted signing above his name. Atty. Talaboc filed several motions for extension but never filed an answer or position paper. Atty. Oliveros filed nothing; notices sent to the address supplied by the OMB were returned unserved, so the IBP sent its March 4, 2019 Order (requiring position papers) to his residence as shown in IBP records. Neither Atty. Talaboc nor Atty. Oliveros attended the mandatory conference.

The Investigating Commissioner counted 95 documents in Atty. Oliveros's name, 132 in Atty. Talaboc's and 104 in Atty. Agcaoili's, all showing only community tax certificates (or nothing) as proof of identity. He found that Atty. Oliveros knew his notarial details were being used and that the two others were negligent in safekeeping theirs, and recommended that each be suspended for six months, have any notarial commission revoked, and be disqualified from being commissioned for two years. The IBP Board of Governors adopted this on March 17, 2022.
issues: Whether respondents are administratively liable for violating the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice for the documents notarized in their names.
Whether Attys. Talaboc and Oliveros are liable for failing to comply with the IBP-CBD's directives, and what penalties apply.
ruling:
**1. No. The OMB failed to prove the notarial charges by substantial evidence.** A lawyer is presumed innocent and presumed to have performed his or her duties in accordance with the oath; the complainant bears the burden of proof by substantial evidence, and mere allegations are not proof. Failure to answer is not an admission. The parts of the OMB Joint Resolution relied on by the Investigating Commissioner were whistleblowers' statements that were "merely the allegations of the complainants" in the OMB case. No notarial register was presented, and there was no proof that respondents consented to the use of their signatures, seals and registers or received money for it.

The documents themselves cast doubt on the commissions used. Certificates in Atty. Talaboc's name lacked her commission serial number, office address, IBP chapter and the place of issue of her PTR (contrary to Rule VIII, Sec. 2 of the Notarial Rules); those in Atty. Agcaoili's name also lacked his Roll of Attorneys number; those in Atty. Oliveros's name lacked the commission serial number and office address. Atty. Agcaoili's certificates claimed a commission valid until December 31, 2009, but the Quezon City RTC certified that he was commissioned only from August 7, 2007 to December 31, 2008 and not since 2009; a one-year commission would violate the two-year term under Rule III, Sec. 11. Certificates in Atty. Oliveros's name stated a commission valid until December 31, 2010, which did not match the Pasig RTC certifications, and his supposed 2010 notarizations bore 2008 IBP and PTR numbers although he had 2010 receipts. The seals and stamps were thus themselves doubtful, and negligence in safekeeping could not be concluded, since others could have had stamps and seals made in respondents' names. "Notaries are not immune from identity theft."

The Court distinguished its rulings penalizing notaries who blamed others, where negligence was shown by giving secretaries full access to notarial paraphernalia or by entries in the notarial books, and *Rigon v. Atty. Subia*, where the notary did not deny the authenticity of his seal. Here there was substantial evidence that respondents' signatures were forged. Atty. Agcaoili's earlier sanctions (*Triol v. Atty. Agcaoili*; *Dionisio, Jr. v. Padernal*) did not involve established forgery.

**2. Yes, as to Attys. Talaboc and Oliveros.** Neither filed an answer or a defense, and neither attended the mandatory conference. Atty. Oliveros is presumed to have received the March 4, 2019 Order under the disputable presumption that a letter duly directed and mailed was received in the regular course of mail (Rule 131, Sec. 3(v)). Following *Kelley v. Atty. Robielos III*, their disregard of the IBP-CBD's directives violated **Canon III, Sec. 2 of the CPRA** and is a less serious offense under Canon VI, Sec. 34(c). For Atty. Oliveros, a first offense (mitigating under Sec. 38(a)(1)) with no aggravating circumstance allowed a fine of not less than half the minimum under Sec. 39: **PHP 17,500.00**. Atty. Talaboc had twice before been sanctioned for ignoring directives to file pleadings (*Completo v. Talaboc*, fine of PHP 10,000.00; *Sia Su v. Talaboc*, three-month suspension); with this aggravating circumstance, she was **suspended for six months**.

The Court added that notarization is not an empty, routinary act but is invested with substantive public interest; still, with the proliferation of fake notaries public, liability for alleged violations of the Notarial Rules must be determined case by case. It reminded Executive Judges of their duty to monitor notaries public, directed the IBP to be more proactive in pursuing fake notaries, and ordered compliance with OCA Circular No. 291-2023 (Task Force Honesto Notario).
disposition: The complaint against Atty. Delfin R. Agcaoili, Jr. was DISMISSED for lack of merit. Atty. Editha P. Talaboc was found GUILTY of violating Canon III of the CPRA and SUSPENDED from the practice of law for six months from receipt of the Decision, with a stern warning, and DIRECTED to file a manifestation that her suspension has started, copy furnished to all courts and quasi-judicial bodies where she has appeared as counsel. Atty. Mark S. Oliveros was found GUILTY of violating Canon III of the CPRA and ORDERED to pay a fine of PHP 17,500.00 within 10 days from receipt, with a stern warning, and to submit proof of payment within 10 days from payment. The OCA was ordered to remind all concerned judges to comply with OCA Circular No. 291-2023, and the Executive Judges of the RTCs of Manila, Quezon City and Pasig, with the OCA and the IBP, were ordered to investigate the notarial services rendered in respondents' names.

bar_questions.q: In a graft investigation, the Ombudsman found that dozens of contracts used to release public funds bore the notarial seal and signature of Atty. Dina, but that she did not actually notarize them. Relying on whistleblowers' statements that she had allowed her seal to be used for a fee, the Ombudsman referred her to the Supreme Court for discipline. Before the IBP, Atty. Dina answered, denying any participation. The notarial certificates on the contracts omit her commission number and office address and state a commission period that conflicts with the certification of the Executive Judge. No notarial register or proof of payment to her was presented. Should Atty. Dina be held liable for violating the Notarial Rules?

alac.answer: No. The charge was not proved by substantial evidence, and the irregularities point to forgery rather than negligence on her part.
alac.legal_basis: In disciplinary proceedings the lawyer is presumed innocent and presumed to have performed her duties in accordance with her oath; the complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence, or such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to justify a conclusion (Rule 133, Sec. 6, Rules on Evidence). Mere allegations are not proof. Where the notarial certificates lack details required by Rule VIII, Sec. 2 of the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice and state commission periods contradicted by official records, the validity of the seals used is doubtful and negligence in safekeeping cannot be presumed, because "[n]otaries are not immune from identity theft" (Re: Resolution Dated August 30, 2017 in OMB-C-C-13-0357 v. Atty. Talaboc, A.C. No. 11889, November 13, 2024).
alac.application: The only evidence that Atty. Dina allowed the use of her seal for a fee is the whistleblowers' statements, which are mere allegations. No notarial register or proof of payment was presented. Meanwhile, the certificates omit her commission number and office address and state a commission period that conflicts with the Executive Judge's certification, which suggests that someone else had a seal and stamp made in her name. Negligence cannot be inferred from these facts.
alac.conclusion: The charge against Atty. Dina for violating the Notarial Rules should be dismissed.

bar_questions.q: Suppose that in the same case Atty. Dina's notarial register, presented before the IBP, contains entries for the questioned contracts, and Atty. Dina admits that the seal on them is genuinely hers. She claims only that her office clerk, who had free access to her seal and register, forged her signature without her knowledge. Would your answer be different?

alac.answer: Yes. Atty. Dina may be held liable for negligence in the handling of her notarial seal and register.
alac.legal_basis: In the Talaboc case (A.C. No. 11889, November 13, 2024), the Court acknowledged its earlier rulings penalizing lawyers who claim that someone else notarized documents in their name, where factors proved the lawyer's negligence, such as allowing secretaries full access to the notarial paraphernalia and the appearance of the notarized documents in the notarial books. It also cited Rigon v. Atty. Subia: where the notary's seal appears on the document and he fails to deny its authenticity, he bears accountability for its use even if done without his consent and knowledge. The Talaboc respondents were exonerated only because these factors were absent and there was substantial evidence that their signatures, and even the commissions stated, were not genuine.
alac.application: Unlike the Talaboc respondents, Atty. Dina admits that the seal is hers, the contracts appear in her own notarial register, and she gave her clerk free access to both. These are the very factors the Court identified as proof of negligence. Even if the clerk forged her signature, the misuse was made possible by her failure to safeguard her notarial paraphernalia.
alac.conclusion: Atty. Dina may be held administratively liable for negligence as a notary public.

bar_questions.q: Atty. Ernie was charged before the IBP Commission on Bar Discipline. He did not file an answer, did not attend the mandatory conference, and did not file a position paper. The IBP order requiring position papers was mailed to his residence as shown in IBP records; he later claimed he never received it. The charge on the merits was eventually dismissed for lack of evidence. (a) May Atty. Ernie still be penalized? (b) If this is his first offense and there is no aggravating circumstance, what is the lowest fine the Court may impose?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. His disregard of the IBP-CBD's directives is a separate violation of Canon III, Sec. 2 of the CPRA, even if the main charge fails. (b) PHP 17,500.00, which is half of the PHP 35,000.00 minimum fine for a less serious offense.
alac.legal_basis: Failing to comply with the IBP-CBD's directives to answer, attend the mandatory conference and file a position paper violates Canon III, Sec. 2 of the CPRA and is a less serious offense under Canon VI, Sec. 34(c), punishable under Sec. 37(b) by suspension of one to six months (or revocation of notarial commission and disqualification of less than two years) or a fine of PHP 35,000.00 to PHP 100,000.00. A first offense is mitigating under Sec. 38(a)(1), and under Sec. 39, if there are mitigating and no aggravating circumstances, the Court may impose a fine not less than half the minimum. A letter duly directed and mailed is presumed received in the regular course of mail (Rule 131, Sec. 3(v)). In Re: Resolution Dated August 30, 2017 in OMB-C-C-13-0357 v. Atty. Talaboc (A.C. No. 11889, November 13, 2024), the notarial charge was dismissed, but Atty. Oliveros was fined PHP 17,500.00 for ignoring the IBP's order.
alac.application: (a) The order was mailed to Atty. Ernie's residence on IBP records, so he is presumed to have received it, and his bare denial does not overcome the presumption. His total non-participation is an infraction against the disciplinary process itself, independent of the merits of the complaint, so the dismissal of the main charge does not absolve him. (b) As a first offender with no aggravating circumstance, he may be fined as low as half of PHP 35,000.00, or PHP 17,500.00.
alac.conclusion: Atty. Ernie may be penalized for violating Canon III, Sec. 2 of the CPRA, with a fine that may go as low as PHP 17,500.00.

notes: Per the decision's own footnote, the "Resolution" in the caption should read "Joint Order." The decision's narration of the IBP mandatory conference dates is internally inconsistent (a conference on December 3, 2019 said to have been reset to January 28, 2019), so those dates are left out. Although the Court said the aggravating circumstance allowed a penalty up to double the maximum, the six-month suspension it imposed on Atty. Talaboc is within the ordinary range for a less serious offense.
